Potsherd
POT-shurd
noun
From pot and the Old English sceard, “a fragment,” a broken piece of earthen vessel.

Biblical Definition

A potsherd is a broken fragment of a fired clay pot, the most common and worthless of refuse, fit only to be cast on the ash-heap or used to scrape and scoop. Job, smitten with sore boils from head to foot, sat down among the ashes and “took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal” (Job 2:8), the picture of a man brought to the dust of utter affliction. The suffering Messiah of the twenty-second Psalm cries, “My strength is dried up like a potsherd” (Psa 22:15), parched and broken in the agony of the cross. Isaiah sets the potsherd against its Maker to rebuke the pride of the creature: “Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth” (Isa 45:9) — as if a shard of clay should contend with the Potter who formed it. Solomon likens flattering lips over a wicked heart to “a potsherd covered with silver dross” (Pro 26:23), a worthless thing glazed to look precious. The potsherd thus teaches the frailty and lowliness of man, who is but clay, easily broken and quickly cast aside; and it magnifies the sovereignty of the Potter, who has power over the clay to make one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour. The shard cannot answer back; it can only be shaped or shattered at the will of Him who made it.

Webster 1828 Definition

A broken fragment of an earthen pot; in Scripture a figure of man’s frailty and lowliness before his Maker.

POTSHERD, a broken piece or fragment of an earthen vessel.

Job took a potsherd to scrape himself in his affliction (Job 2:8).

The suffering Messiah’s strength is dried like a potsherd (Psa 22:15).

The potsherd may not strive with the Potter who formed it (Isa 45:9).

Flattery over a wicked heart is a potsherd glazed with silver dross (Pro 26:23).

Key Scripture

Job 2:8 — "And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes."

Psa 22:15 — "My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death."

Isa 45:9 — "Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands?"

Pro 26:23 — "Burning lips and a wicked heart are like a potsherd covered with silver dross."

Modern Corruption

A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses the frailty of man and the sovereignty of the Potter.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the sovereignty of the Potter over the clay. A potsherd is but a broken shard of fired earth, and Isaiah’s woe falls upon the creature who would strive with the Maker that formed him: shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? Man, who is dust, has no standing to contend with God over His decrees; the shard cannot answer the hand that shaped it. To know oneself a potsherd is the beginning of humility before the throne.

The potsherd also preaches the frailty of our estate and the depth of Christ’s sufferings. Job sat in the ashes and scraped his sores with a shard; the Saviour cried that His strength was dried up like a potsherd as He was brought into the dust of death. Our days are brittle as fired clay, soon broken and cast aside; and the Lord of glory was content to be made low as a potsherd, that He might lift His people from the ash-heap and make of broken clay a vessel unto honour.

Hebrew Roots

The word joins pot and sherd, a fragment, naming a broken piece of earthen vessel.

Potsherd — pot + Old English sceard, “a fragment.”

It is a broken shard of fired clay, common refuse.

Job scraped his boils with a potsherd in the ashes.

The potsherd may not strive with the Potter who made it.

It figures the frailty and lowliness of man before God.

Usage

"Like a potsherd, man is but brittle clay, easily broken and quickly cast aside."

"The potsherd that may not strive with its Maker rebukes all pride against God’s sovereign decrees."

"Christ’s strength dried like a potsherd shows how low the Saviour stooped to raise His people."
